# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm, Comment)

Sections 1–5 of this comment are valuable. Using the microdata, it shows:
- **Attrition:** Halden described its withdrawals inaccurately.
- **Output measure:** managers' indices exceeded their own records in 19 of 23 cases.
- **Hours:** about 30% of the "scheduled" hours reduction did not happen.
- **Revenue:** Halden's revenue rise was nominal.

The corrected estimate of +10.8% is careful work, and the data note is commendably candid.

The final step does not hold up. The jump from "the gain is about 11%, not 23%" to "per-hour gains are entirely an artifact" rests on a weak novelty argument. It also cites only the half of the Varden trial that supports the comment, and the other half contradicts that conclusion.

## Arithmetic

Most figures check out:
- Table 2: 98.7/0.8 = 1.234; 95.1/0.8 = 1.189; 98.4/0.859 = 1.146; 95.4/0.861 = 1.108.
- Hours ratios: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 ≈ 0.974, a fall of 2.6%.
- The "roughly four points" and "roughly six points" figures in the conclusion are right.

There are two errors.

**1. The hours breakdown in §3 doesn't add up.**
- Scheduled hours were 32. Adding +0.7 h on each of four days (2.8 h) and 1.6 h on the day off gives about **36.4 h**. Measuring the +0.7 against baseline days of about 8.06 h instead gives about 36.6 h.
- The reported pilot average is **34.6 h**. To reach that, the longer days would need to add about 1.0 h a week, roughly 0.25 h a day.
- So either the per-day figure or the average is wrong. The 34.6 feeds Table 2, so this needs resolving.

**2. The novelty extrapolation gives about month nine, not "around month ten."**
- Energy fell from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6, a decline of about 0.107 SD per month.
- At that rate, 0.29 reaches zero after about 2.7 more months, which is month 8.7.
- The difference is small, but see point 3 below on whether extrapolating from two points is meaningful at all.

## Main issues

**1. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own estimate.**
- The comment's best corrected figure is **+10.8%**, which is positive and given without a confidence interval.
- The abstract says the four problems "account for *most*" of the gain. The conclusion says "*entirely*." Those are different claims.
- Only one of the four problems, attrition, is left unquantified. "Plausibly" novelty is an argument, not an estimate.
- The final sentence also widens the claim from the Halden pilot to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes." That covers studies the comment has not re-analysed, including Varden.

**2. The comment cites only half of the Varden trial.**
- It calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention the case-processing stratum of the same trial.
- That stratum found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)** at **nine months**. That is three months later than Halden, and past the point where the comment's extrapolation says the novelty effect would have run out.
- It was randomised, used record-based output and timesheet hours, and its staff did not choose the change. It already avoids the problems the comment identifies.
- Varden's 12.5% is strikingly close to the comment's corrected 10.8% for Halden. Two very different designs agreeing on about 11–12% is, if anything, evidence of a real effect in work not tied to presence.
- The comment cannot treat Varden as the most reliable evidence for one conclusion and ignore it on the other.

**3. The novelty argument is weak, and the comment doesn't use the data that could test it.**
- Fitting a straight line through two survey points assumes decay continues at a constant rate to zero. The decline could equally level off at a positive value.
- Self-reported energy is also not output. The comment assumes the output gain tracks energy without showing it.
- More importantly, **Halden collected the output index monthly.** The microdata should show directly whether output per hour fell between months 1 and 6, at least for the 17 organisations with records and time tracking. That is the obvious test of novelty, and the comment does not run it.
- The burden-of-proof argument at the end of §6 is a rhetorical move, not evidence.

**4. Table 2 changes the correction and the subset at the same time.**
- Row 1 covers all 61 organisations; the other rows cover 23, 27 and 17.
- So the fall from 23.4% to 10.8% mixes the effect of the corrections with differences in which organisations are included.
- The overlap may be small, since manager indices are similar across subsets (98.7, 98.9 and 98.4). But the clean comparison is easy: within the 17, show the as-reported figure (manager index ÷ 0.8) next to the corrected one.
- The data note acknowledges the subset problem, but the abstract presents the fall as a pure correction.

**5. The cost of attrition is described but not estimated.**
- §1 is an important finding. It shows that Halden's description of the withdrawals ("during the preparation phase") was inaccurate, and Halden should be asked to respond.
- However, the comment does not bound how much attrition matters. It could use the withdrawers' size and any partial output data, or simple worst-case assumptions.
- Nine organisations out of 70 can lower the pooled estimate, but by an amount that depends on their size and results. Without a bound, attrition can't support "entirely."

**6. Some "record-based" output measures may themselves measure hours.**
- The examples of record-based output include **billable hours delivered**. In professional services that is a measure of time, not of output.
- Dividing billable hours by actual hours gives the share of time that is billable. Reduced schedules could raise this share by cutting non-billable time, with no change in how productive each hour is.
- The comment should say how many of the 23 organisations used hours-based measures, and check whether the results hold without them.

**7. The critique of Varden's meetings analysis misdescribes it and applies a double standard.**
- Varden did not "select" the seven offices. They are all the treated case-processing offices.
- The meeting data were collected at month six, before the nine-month results were known.
- Varden's authors themselves said the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.
- The comment's caution is reasonable, but it overstates what Varden claimed. It also rejects a seven-office correlation as non-replicable while resting its own novelty case on a two-point extrapolation.

## Smaller points

- **Revenue deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue; an output-price index for each sector would be better. The country and source of the 4.1% figure should be stated. The overall point stands either way.
- **Retail.** The −11.2% retail figure comes from three organisations. It is consistent with Varden's counter result, but it is too small to lean on.
- **Coverage-bound work.** The conclusion that "where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is well supported, but it is conditional on design. Varden kept headcount and opening hours fixed. Hiring to restore coverage would change the outcome, and the cost.
- **Recommendations.** These are sound. The call to analyse everyone who enrolled, including those who withdraw, matters most.

## How the three papers fit together

| | Halden (pilot) | Varden (RCT) | Varga & Holm (re-analysis) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, work not tied to presence | +23.4% (scheduled hours, manager output) | +12.5% (actual hours, records, 9 months) | +10.8% (actual hours, records, subset) |
| Work tied to presence | "Sector-general" | Output per employee −11.4%, worse service | Retail output −11.2% (n = 3) |
| Interpretation | Large, universal gain | Depends on whether output needs presence | "Entirely an artifact" |

The best-supported position lies between Halden's and the comment's:
- **Work tied to presence:** reduced hours with fixed staffing lower output and service.
- **Other work:** a gain of roughly 10–12% per actual hour is supported by two independent designs, with durability beyond about nine months not yet established.

Varden's 24-month follow-up, and a month-by-month analysis of Halden's output data, are the obvious next tests.

I can draft this as a formal referee report on the comment or as a short synthesis note across the three papers.
